meta: Thomas de Keyser's portrait of three children and a man, signed in August 1622 and bought for the Rijksmuseum in 1891.
about: Three children stand in the foreground beside a globe and a table with jewels on it. A man stands behind a balustrade in the background. Thomas de Keyser signed and dated the painting above the hand that holds the youngest child's wrist, and he added the month, August 1622. In April 1891 Dr Abraham Bredius bought it in England for the museum, paying 1,270 guilders.

meta: Zhao Mengfu Writing the Heart Sutra in Exchange for Tea, a handscroll painted by Qiu Ying in 1542 and 1543.
about: The Yuan calligrapher Zhao Mengfu is said to have copied the Heart Sutra for a priest named Li in return for tea. Qiu Ying, a professional painter from Suzhou, painted the scene in the Ming period for his patron. Zhao holds a brush with paper laid out before him. On the table are an ink stone, an ink stick and a small water dropper. Drops of water dissolve the ink stick into liquid ink as it is ground on the flat stone.

meta: The Death of Brutus, Pierre-Narcisse Guérin's 1793 painting of the dead Roman conspirator carried aloft.
about: The corpse of Marcus Junius Brutus, one of the leaders of the plot against Julius Caesar, is carried aloft after his suicide. He had been defeated at the Battle of Philippi. Pierre-Narcisse Guérin painted it in 1793 as his first entry for the Prix de Rome. The work is in the Musée de la Révolution française in Vizille.

meta: Sofonisba Anguissola's self-portrait at an easel, painted around 1556 and now at Łańcut Castle.
about: The painter shows herself at work on a devotional canvas. The picture dates from about 1556 to 1565 and is now in Łańcut Castle in Poland. It comes from the same period as her Self-Portrait at a Spinet in Naples. It belongs to a group of self-portraits that also includes the one in Vienna and a miniature in Boston.

meta: Giovanni Girolamo Savoldo's altarpiece of the Madonna and Child with four saints, painted for San Domenico in Pesaro and now in the Brera.
about: The Madonna and Child sit between two angels playing music. Below them, from left to right, stand Saint Peter, Saint Dominic, Saint Paul and Saint Jerome. Giovanni Girolamo Savoldo painted the panel around 1524 to 1526. It is in the Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan. He made another work for San Domenico in the same years, Rest on the Flight into Egypt, which is now in a private collection in Milan.

meta: Sophie Crouzet, painted by Louis Hersent around 1801 in a sheer white dress, at the Cleveland Museum of Art.
about: The sitter's dress deliberately recalls ancient Roman costume. White muslin and a plain cut also come from earlier English fashions, which preferred simplicity to the elaborate colorful clothes of the early 1700s. The museum adds that the transparency of the dress carried political meaning. After the French Revolution began in 1789, costume signaled allegiance. For women, transparency became more literal, as in the sheer fabric worn by Crouzet, who came from a family of active revolutionaries. She was a first cousin of the artist.

meta: Pedro Berruguete's portrait of Pope Sixtus IV, painted from life in Rome in the 1470s or 1480s.
about: The pope raises his hand in blessing and meets the viewer's gaze. Pedro Berruguete spent about ten years in Italy in the 1470s and 1480s, and in Rome he painted Sixtus IV della Rovere from life. White highlights make the jewelled garments glitter, and the triregnum, the triple crown that marks the papacy, gets the same treatment. In the late 19th century the American critic and collector James Jackson Jarves owned the painting.

meta: Coming South, Tom Roberts's 1886 painting of migrants arriving in Australia by steamship, bought by the National Gallery of Victoria in 1967.
about: Migrants from Europe travel to Australia aboard a steamship in this painting. Tom Roberts based it on sketches he made in 1885, when he sailed home on the SS Lusitania after four years in Europe. The National Gallery of Victoria calls it a definitive image of the migrant experience and Roberts's first exploration of one of the great themes of Australian life. The gallery acquired it in 1967.

meta: The kneeling founder as a pilgrim to Jerusalem with Saint James, the left wing of Aertgen Claesz van Leyden's triptych with the Raising of Lazarus.
about: The donor kneels in worship as a pilgrim to Jerusalem, with a palm branch, while Saint James the Greater stands behind him. This is the left wing of a triptych. The central panel shows the raising of Lazarus, and the right wing is kept with it in the Rijksmuseum. The wing was sold in Berlin in 1912, together with its pendant. At a London sale in 1980 it was offered as the work of Cornelis Engebrechtsz, and the museum bought it for 9,000 pounds with support from the Rijksmuseum-Stichting.

meta: De Rot, Adriaan van der Hoop's trotting horse, painted by Anthony Oberman at the coach house in Santpoort in 1828.
about: A racehorse or trotter named De Rot stands by the coach house in Santpoort with a blanket over its back. De Rot belonged to Adriaan van der Hoop. In the background a man stands near a carriage, and a bucket sits at the left. Anthony Oberman signed and dated the painting at the lower left in 1828. It is on loan from the City of Amsterdam, from the A. van der Hoop Bequest.

meta: Charles-François Pinceloup de la Grange, a 1747 portrait by Jean-Baptiste Perronneau at the Getty.
about: Charles-François Pinceloup de la Grange wears elegant clothes and a powdered wig. He raises his head slightly and gazes into the distance. He belonged to the nobility of Orléans and had recently received several prestigious government appointments. The Getty thinks this portrait and a matching one of his wife may have been made to celebrate his success. Jean-Baptiste Perronneau painted it near the start of his career. He worked mostly in pastel.

meta: Village Festival, David Teniers the Younger's painting of dancing and music among peasants, at the Cleveland Museum of Art.
about: Peasant festivals became a very popular subject for Flemish artists in the 1600s. David Teniers the Younger painted peasants dancing and playing music, and he concentrated on the cheerful side of their lives. His pictures often show close family groups at the celebration. Earlier painters tended to show broken and disorderly objects. Teniers painted household items in brass, ceramic and glass in perfect condition, which the museum reads as a sign of the peasants' growing prosperity. Surviving drawings show he sketched many peasants from life.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Noah L. Butkin

meta: The Last Day of Pompeii, Karl Bryullov's large painting of Vesuvius erupting, made between 1830 and 1833.
about: The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 is the subject of this large history painting. Karl Bryullov worked on it from 1830 to 1833. It sits between Neoclassicism, which ruled in Russia then, and the Romanticism then spreading in France. Nearly everyone welcomed it. It made Bryullov the first Russian painter with an international reputation, and it inspired Edward Bulwer-Lytton's novel The Last Days of Pompeii. Critics in France and Russia did observe that the perfectly modelled bodies seemed at odds with the people's desperate plight.

meta: Piero di Cosimo's Visitation with Saints Nicholas and Anthony, made for a Capponi chapel in Florence and given to the National Gallery of Art in 1939.
about: The Capponi family commissioned this panel around 1490 for their chapel of Saint Nicholas in the church of Santo Spirito in Florence. Giorgio Vasari described it, and singled out Saint Anthony with a pair of spectacles on his nose. In 1713 it moved to the Villa Capponi at Legnaia. Frederick West bought it about 1850 and took it to Chirk Castle in Wales, and his descendants sold it in 1891. Duveen Brothers passed it to Samuel H. Kress, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1939.
